TITLE: Time Series Data Quality Estimation via LLM-Prompted Assessment
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of pre-trained LLMs with carefully designed prompts to estimate time series data quality, focusing on electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, and traffic forecasting. We will fine-tune the existing 175B parmerters T5 model and design a set of new prompts that capture desirable time series quality criteria such as temporal smoothness, distributions, and monotonicity.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline models such as TimeShap and TimeInf, as well as ablations of different prompt designs.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The LLM-prompted approach is competitive with existing methods, but may struggle to capture nuanced aspects of temporal dependencies, requiring further investigation.

This proposal focuses on an LLM-based approach, which leverages pre-trained models and custom-designed prompts to estimate time series quality. The goal is to demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on real-world datasets from various domains. By comparing the results with existing methods and ablation studies, we can gain insight into the strengths and limitations of the proposed approach.

TITLE: Evaluating the Privacy-Utility Trade-off of Adversarially Trained Anonymizers
PROPOSAL: Compare three anonymizer models trained on synthetic online comment data:
    1. An large, proprietary LLM (GPT-4) used as a baseline.
    2. A feedback-guided adversarial anonymizer using two separate LLMs, similar to prior work.
    3. A small, locally run anonymizer trained without external adversarial feedback, to test its performance without relying on propietary models.
We will measure their privacy-utility trade-off via a set of metrics, including attribute inference accuracy and the Kendall's W correlation coefficient of modified text READABILITY.
CONTROLS: Include ablations with varying levels of anonymizer capability (e.g., a less capable anonymizer that removes only explicit names) and trained without adversarial feedback to see the impact on inference accuracy in downstream models.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: While the large GPT-4 baseline should perform well, it will not achieve a fair privacy-utility trade-off due to intense compute requirements. The small, locally run anonymizer should provide a balance between privacy and utility, potentially beating the feedback-guided approach on text readability without sacrificing too much in terms of privacy. However, its performance might degrade on complex inference tasks (e.g., inferring author location from text cues), potentially failing to scale over more challenging scenarios.

TITLE: Reducing Memorization and Inference Threats with Synthetic Data Generators

We will train five anonymizer models:
    1. A baseline model trained on real anonymized online comments with enumerated attribute values.
    2. A prior anonymizer model from experiment 1 (1).
    3. Three models trained on synthetic data: 
        a. One with enumerated attribute values.
        b. One with masked, numeric attribute values.
        c. One with adjective/ adverb descriptor pairs for attribute values, instead of numeric or descriptive enumerations
We measure the trade-off between attribute inference accuracy and synthetic data's semantic coherence, aiming to understand whether well-benchmarked synthetic data can safeguard privacy effectively enough.
CONTROLS: Investigate how the number, diversity, and quality of synthetic comments, and the type of attribute masking or enumeration affect the anonymizers' performance, and validate our approach with a human evaluation of synthetic comments' credibility.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Synthetic data will indeed help to mitigate memorization and inference threats, making low-resource anonymizers more robust without significantly impacting utility. However, we might experience difficulties in masking some attributes (e.g., age), which will otherwise require sophisticated strategies (e.g., generating age-profiles), where things might fail in recognition/ inferring the privacy objectives.

TITLE: Non-asymptotic Guarantees for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We will derive a non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantee for the KernelSHAP estimator, providing an upper bound on the number of subset samples required to achieve a certain level of accuracy. The guarantee is formulated in terms of the Lipschitz constant of the regression problem, the kernel weights, and the required accuracy.
CONTROLS: We compare the derived upper bound with existing bounds for LeverageSHAP, and evaluate the performance of the derived sample complexity guarantee on real-world datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to derive an upper bound that provides a guaranteed accuracy guarantee for KernelSHAP, which can be used to inform the design of experiments for evaluating the estimator's performance. The guarantee may be pessimistic, particularly for small d, as it will not account for the effective dimensionality reduction provided by the kernel weighting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Randomized Subset Sampling for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of randomized subset sampling methods on the sample complexity of KernelSHAP. Specifically, we will compare the performance of sampling with replacement, sampling without replacement, and the paired sampling strategy currently used in the SHAP library implementation. We will derive bounds on the reduction in sample complexity achieved by these methods and evaluate their practical performance on real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare the bounds derived in the previous proposal (1) with the sample complexity achieved by the various subset sampling methods, and we also consider the approximate Shapley values estimator currently used in the SHAP library implementation.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that the paired sampling strategy achieves significant reductions in sample complexity over uniform sampling, and that these reductions are comparable to those achieved by LeverageSHAP. However, we also expect that the benefits of paired sampling may come at the cost of increased computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymptotic Analysis of Unbiased KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We will provide an asymptotic analysis of the Unbiased KernelSHAP estimator, which is an unbiased variant of the KernelSHAP estimator. We will derive an asymptotic variance bound for the estimator and study the bias-variance tradeoff. This analysis will provide insights into the relative performance of Unbiased KernelSHAP and KernelSHAP, and help understand why Unbiased KernelSHAP may underperform the original KernelSHAP in practice.
CONTROLS: We compare the derived asymptotic variance bound with previous bounds for Unbiased KernelSHAP, and evaluate the empirical performance of Unbiased KernelSHAP and KernelSHAP on real-world datasets.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to show that the asymptotic variance bound of Unbiased KernelSHAP grows faster than that of KernelSHAP, which can explain the observed underperformance. However, we also expect that the asymptotic analysis may not fully capture the behavior of the estimators in small samples, where the bias of Unbiased KernelSHAP may be too high to be negligible.

TITLE: Investigating Basic Schrödinger Bridge Formulations for Unimodal Trajectories

We will train Schrödinger bridge models with known unimodal trajectories for the task of reconstructing the intermediate steps, evaluating model performance using metrics such as the mean squared error and probability density estimate of the bridge path against ground truth. Controls will include sampling without replacement and ablations without the non-linear state cost term.
